title: Recreating viable YY^h genotype uncovers the role of CpYYL underlying YY lethality in papaya

paper_content.abstract: Papaya is a trioecious species with XX females, XY males, and XYh hermaphrodites. Any combination of Y and Yh chromosomes is lethal. The gene underlying YY lethality is pivotal in the transition from stage 2 to stage 3 in sex chromosome evolution. Here, we identify and functionally validate the YY lethality gene in papaya, CpYYL. Loss of CpYYL function accelerates glycolysis and reduces sucrose accumulation in embryo, causing embryo abortion. CpYYL interacts with CpAKRP and overexpression of both genes partially rescues seed abortion in the heterozygous emb506 and akrp mutants, indicating conserved role in plastid differentiation and embryo development. Viable YYh and YhYh plants are generated through genetic engineering and crossing, although both genotypes show high seedling mortality. Crossing YYh male with XX female papaya shows 1:1 ratio of male to hermaphrodite plants without recombination between MSY and HSY. Identification of CpYYL fills a critical gap in papaya sex chromosome evolution, and provides new resources for genomic and epigenetic studies.
paper_content.introduction:
Papaya (Carica papaya L., 2n=2x=18) is a fast-growing fruit crop known for its palatable flavor, rich nutritional profile, and versatile culinary and medicinal applications. It is native to Central America and southern Mexico and is now cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions worldwide. The papaya fruit is a large, fleshy berry that varies in size, shape, and color depending on the variety. Papaya pulp is rich in provitamin A, vitamin C, and other essential nutrients, making it a popular choice for fresh consumption and processed products like juices, jams, and dried fruit. The protease enzyme papain is widely used in the food, pharmaceutical, and cosmetic industries. Papaya has been recommended as a dietary intervention to prevent vitamin A deficiency in developing countries1.

Papaya is a diploid species with 9 chromosomes and a genome size of 352Mb2. Transgenic papaya has been widely publicized as a success story that saved the papaya industry from an epidemic of papaya ringspot virus (PRSV)3,4. Since the devastating PRSV disease has been effectively controlled, the primary problem for papaya production is the segregation of sex types. In most papaya-producing regions, hermaphrodites are preferred due to their higher productivity and compact, pear-shaped fruits, which reduce shipping costs by 20%. However, the progeny from self-fertilized hermaphrodites segregate in a 2:1 ratio (two hermaphrodites to one female), while progeny from female trees pollinated by hermaphrodites segregate in a 1:1 ratio (one hermaphrodite to one female). This occurs because YhYh embryos are nonviable. Farmers relying on hermaphrodites for production need to plant at least five seedlings per planting hill and wait 4–6 months until flowering. Thinning is then performed to maximize the number of hermaphrodite plants. This practice is labor-intensive and inefficient, resulting in wasted time, water, and nutrients while delaying production due to competition among the plants in early growth. This has been a problem since the beginning of papaya cultivation that persists to this day5. Identifying the gene responsible for YY lethality could pave the way for engineering viable YYh and YhYh genotypes. These genotypes are essential germplasms for developing true-breeding hermaphrodite cultivars by crossing XX females with YhYh hermaphrodites.

Dioecy and sex chromosomes are common in animals but rare in plants, occurring in approximately 10% land plant species and 6% of flowering plant species6,7. The evolution of sex chromosomes can be categorized into six stages. Stage 3 involves the expansion of the male-specific region due to the accumulation of retrotransposons, translocation and duplication of genomic fragments. This process is accompanied by Y chromosome degeneration, resulting in the lethality of the YY genotype. Consequently, males are restricted to the heterozygous XY genotype, as observed in papaya6.

Cultivated hermaphrodite papaya was selected from a male population in Central America about 4000 years ago, resulting in a modified Yh chromosome8. The male- and hermaphrodite-specific region of the Y and Yh chromosomes (MSY and HSY) has been sequenced9. The identity of MSY and HSY is 99.6%, indicating they share a common ancestral MSY recently8.

Extensively studied plant sex chromosomes include those of white campion (Silene latifolia Poir.)10–12, papaya8,9, and asparagus (Asparagus officinalis L.)13,14. The successful assembly of the asparagus YY genome led to the identification of two sex determination genes in the asparagus MSY14. A major challenge in studying MSY in papaya and white campion is the unavailability of YY genotype. In the XY genotype, the X chromosome does not recombine with MSY, rendering genes in MSY genetically unmappable15,16. This limitation could be overcome if viable YY genotypes of papaya could be recreated.

Classical genetic analyses led to the hypothesis of five factors in the sex determination region, contributing to distinctive morphologies among the three sex types in papaya17. 1. Mp, male peduncle, responsible for the long, ramified, many-flowered cymose inflorescence of male trees; 2. l, zygotic lethal (i.e., YY lethality); 3. sa, suppressor of the androecium; 4. sg, suppressor of the gynoecium; 5. C, hypothetical factor for recombination suppression in the sex determining region. We have discovered that the factor C is two inversions that occurred 7 and 1.9 million years ago (mya), respectively9. Together, these five factors—four genes and two chromosomal rearrangements—are essential for papaya sex chromosomes to reach stage 3, characterized by YY lethality. The objectives of this study are to identify the YY lethality gene and generate viable YhYh hermaphrodites for papaya improvement.

In this work, we identify CpYYL as the gene responsible for YY lethality in papaya, a defining feature of its evolved sex chromosomes. Using transgenic complementation, we generate viable YYh and YhYh plants, providing critical resources for dissecting sex chromosome recombination. We further demonstrate that CpYYL interacts with CpAKRP and that loss of CpYYL disrupts sucrose metabolism, leading to embryo abortion. These findings directly link the degeneration of an essential gene on the Y chromosome to the stabilization of dioecy, offering evolutionary insights and valuable germplasm for papaya genetic studies and crop improvement.
paper_content.results:
Identification of a candidate gene controlling YY lethality
Papaya has three sex genotypes: female (XX), hermaphrodite (XYh) and male (XY), each exhibiting distinct floral features (Fig. 1a–c). Self-pollinated hermaphrodite flowers showed a segregation ratio of 2 XYh hermaphrodites to 1 XX female, with ~25% of seeds aborted due to YhYh lethality, lacking discernible embryos (Fig. 1d, e). The aborted YhYh genotype seeds had no discernible embryos (Fig. 1f,g). In contrast, fertilizing female flowers with hermaphrodite pollen resulted in a 1 XYh hermaphrodite to 1 XX female ratio without seed abortion (Fig. 1d, e and Supplementary Table 1).

Papaya ovules exhibited retrograde development, with early and late globular embryos forming at 35 and 49 days post-pollination, respectively. Heart embryos at 65 days, followed by torpedo stage at 72 days, and cotyledon stage at 79 days (Supplementary Fig. 1). However, aborted embryos of the YhYh genotype exhibited phenotypic differences from their normal counterparts. Up to 50 days after pollination (DAP), embryos of the YhYh genotype were indistinguishable from normal XYh embryos. However, as wild-type embryos progressed to the cotyledon stage, YhYh embryos exhibited degeneration of embryo and endosperm (Fig. 1f–i).

Given the lethal phenotype observed in YY/YhYh individuals, we hypothesize that the gene responsible for YY/YhYh lethality remains functional in the X chromosome but becomes non-functional in the MSY and HSY. To investigate this, we screened 34 X-specific genes9 (Supplementary Data 1). Functional annotation identified PYhCpXYh7 encodes an ankyrin repeat domain-containing protein orthologous to Arabidopsis EMB506, which is an essential gene for normal embryo development18. Transcriptomic analysis revealed CpEMB506 is highly expressed across four embryonic stages, with its expression level gradually declining as development proceeds (Supplementary Data 1). The gene function and expression pattern made CpEMB506 as a strong candidate gene underlying YY, YYh, and YhYh lethality. The X allele features a large first intron of 8374 bp, which includes DNA transposons and LTR retrotransposons. In contrast, the HSY allele has lost the first exon (409 bp) and 7352 bp in the first intron, rendering it a pseudogene (Fig. 2a, b). A comparison of the coding DNA sequences of X, HSY, and MSY alleles revealed that the disrupted MSY and HSY alleles share conserved sequences, but differ from the X allele by SNPs and Indels (Supplementary Fig. 2). Further quantitative PCR and RNA-seq data showed that the CpEMB506-X allele is expressed in both embryos and female flowers, whereas Cpemb506-HSY pseudogene is not expressed (Supplementary Fig. 3).

Validation of CpEMB506 function and generation of viable YhYh and YYh papaya plants
To validate the function of CpEMB506, we generated transgenic plants expressing CpEMB506 under its native promoter to assess its ability to rescue the abortion phenotype in YhYh seeds. The pOX vector was transformed into papaya cultivar “Zhonghuang” (ZH) calli using an efficient genetic transformation system (Supplementary Fig. 4). Transgenic lines of ProCpEMB506::CpEMB506/ZH (CpEMB506Pro/ZH) female plants were generated and confirmed via PCR (Supplementary Fig. 5).

These transgenic females were crossed with pollen from hermaphrodite cultivars pollen, producing hermaphrodite F1 plants named transCpEMB506 XYh (ProCpEMB506::CpEMB506/F1 XYh). These F1 plants were then self-pollinated to produce a segregating F2 population, which was subsequently screened to identify YhYh genotype plants (Supplementary Fig. 6). All F2 seeds exhibited black seeds, with no presence of white aborted seeds. In contrast, the control hermaphrodite seeds showed aborted white seeds, indicating that the phenotype of aborted seeds in hermaphroditic plants was partially restored (Fig. 2c). YYh genotype was obtained by crossing CpEMB506Pro/ZH XYh with ZH XY or AU9 XY male plants (Supplementary Fig. 7).

Next, two F2 populations were developed from two test crosses for identifying YhYh and YYh genotype plants, 20–1 population derived from a cross between a “SunUp” female and a 20-1 YYh male, and 15–4 population derived from a cross between a ZH female and a 15-4 YYh male. We identified 94 YYh seedlings from 20–1 population, and 32 YYh from 15–4 population after testing 4652 and 1386 F2 individuals, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 8 and Supplementary Data 2). However, only 18 YhYh plants were identified in the 20–1 population, with no such individuals detected in the 15–4 population (Supplementary Fig. 8 and Supplementary Data 2). All YYh and YhYh were identified using the developed sex-specific CpEMB506, PYhCpXYh31 and TE markers. These markers effectively distinguish between female and hermaphrodite plants, as well as between male and hermaphrodite plants (Supplementary Tables 2 and 3). To further validate the accuracy of the YhYh genotype, we conducted next-generation resequencing on six YhYh plants and eight YYh as control. Sequencing results confirmed the absence of the X-linked sex determination region in all assayed plants (Fig. 2d). We aligned the sequencing data to the AU9 MSY genome as the reference and analyzed 15 high-confidence SNP markers located within the MSY. Genotype analysis revealed that all six YhYh samples matched the HSY genotype, verifying the accuracy of YhYh genotype identification (Supplementary Figs. 9, 10 and Supplementary Data 3). However, all 18 YhYh seedlings and 32 of the 126 YYh seedlings displayed reduced viability, with post-embryonic developmental arrest occurring in 100% of YhYh and 25.4% of YYh individuals (Supplementary Data 2). We observed that the apex of 18 YhYh and 32 YYh seedlings gradually ceased development, leaving only the stem, and eventually, the seedlings died after approximately 10 days of growth (Fig. 2e).

The YYh genotype plants exhibited a male phenotype. Comparative analysis of YYh and XY male plants showed no significant differences in plant height, flower structure, and peduncle length compared to XY males (two-tailed t-test, p=0.14–0.97) (Fig. 2f–i and Supplementary Fig. 11). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) confirmed that pollen morphology and vitality were identical between YYh and XY male flowers (Supplementary Fig. 12).

FISH analysis revealed that the Y-chromosome-specific probe generated one strong signal in one Yh chromosome in XYh hermaphrodite “SunUp”, and two strong signals in two YYh individuals, confirming that the fertility of YYh was restored (Fig. 2j to l). These results validated that CpEMB506 is the gene controlling YY, YYh, YhYh lethality. We renamed this YY lethality gene CpEMB506 as CpYYL.

The CpYYL is expressed in embryo and encodes a chloroplast localized protein
To elucidate the physiological function of CpYYL, its expression was examined across various papaya tissues. CpYYL was expressed in leaves, roots, stems, and at two floral developmental stages of male, hermaphrodite, and female plants. Expression was markedly higher in flowers, especially in female flowers and their pistils (Supplementary Fig. 13a). The highest expression level was observed in ovules from fruit 5–15 DAP. As ovules developed, expression gradually decreased, with a sharp decline at 35 DAP (Supplementary Fig. 13b).

To further validate spatial expression patterns, we performed in situ hybridization of CpYYL in embryos. Strong hybridization signals were detected in both the early globular embryo and the endotesta at 35 DAP, whereas weaker signals were observed in globular-shaped embryo and endotesta at 50 DAP (Fig. 3a–f), indicated that CpYYL functions in early embryo development.

AtEMB506 protein is localized in the chloroplast, and has a chloroplast targeting signal peptide19. The investigation of subcellular localization of CpYYL displayed CpYYL-GFP was co-localized with the chlorophyll fluorescence signals (Fig. 3i,k), indicating a chloroplast localization. However, when we deleted the putative signal peptide of 41 amino acids directing CpYYL to plastids, CpYYL-del-GFP was irregularly distributed on the cell membrane and not co-localized with the chlorophyll fluorescence signals, confirming the existence of a signal peptide for targeting CpYYL to the chloroplasts (Fig. 3j).

The mutation of CpYYL impacts the expression of genes in sucrose metabolism
To evaluate the impact of CpYYL loss on gene expression, we conducted RNA-seq analysis on ovules at different developmental stages from crosses between “Zhongbai” XX female and XYh hermaphrodites, as well as from self-pollinated XYh hermaphrodites. Because it is not possible to distinguish aborted seeds in self-pollinated hermaphrodite fruit based on phenotype before seed maturation, we included both cross types in the analysis. A total of 50, 524, 801, and 39 DEGs detected at 5, 15, 35, and 65 DAP ovules between ovules of Zhongbai females from the cross and Zhongbai hermaphrodites from self-pollinated plants (Fig. 4a).

We identified 412 and 683 unigenes expressed at 15 and 35 DAP (Fig. 4b). Our focus was on genes specifically expressed at the 15-day stage between female and hermaphrodite ovules. Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis revealed that the downregulated DEGs were mainly enriched in post-embryonic morphogenesis, succinate transport, oxidation-reduction process and hormone stimulus response. In contrast, the upregulated DEGs are primarily associated with precursor metabolites and energy, pyruvate metabolic and glycolytic processes (Fig. 4c). Further analysis using the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) indicated that the downregulated DEGs were mainly enriched in pathways related to carbon fixation via the Calvin cycle, glycolysis, and starch and sucrose metabolism (Fig. 4d).

Sucrose metabolism provide energy for embryonic development20–22. The key enzymes involved in this process, including alkaline/neutral invertases (A/N-Inv-C), which are localized in the mitochondria, and catalyzes the breakdown of sucrose into glucose and fructose, thereby fueling various cellular processes23. Additionally, a suite of other enzymes, including hexokinase 4 (HXK4), cytoplasmic phosphoglucose isomerase (CPGI), PFK3, fructose-1,6-bisphosphate aldolase (FBA6)24, fructokinase (FRK), triosephosphate isomerase (TPI), and fructose-bisphosphate aldolase 6 (FBA6)25, plays significant roles in this metabolic cascade. The genes encoding these enzymes all showed increased transcription in 15-day hermaphrodite ovules (Fig. 4e, f), which in turn accelerates the glycolytic pathway. This metabolic shift is further underscored by the observation of significantly reduced sucrose content in hermaphrodites at the 15-day stage (Fig. 4g, h, Supplementary Fig. 14, and Supplementary Data 4, 5), highlighting the dynamic changes in energy metabolism during this critical developmental phase.

CpYYL interact with CpAKRP during the papaya life cycle
To explore the molecular mechanisms underlying protein interaction involving CpYYL, we screened for potential interacting proteins. Yeast two-hybrid analysis revealed a strong interaction between CpYYL and an ankyrin repeat protein, CpAKRP (Fig. 5a, b). AKRP is crucial in the initial differentiation of the proplastid19. Domain interaction analysis using truncated domains of CpYYL and CpAKRP showed that the interaction was markedly weakened when only the N-terminal regions of both proteins were present, whereas efficient binding required the four ankyrin (ANK) domain repeats along with its upstream region (Supplementary Fig. 15).

Subsequent BiFC-assays confirmed the in vivo interaction between CpYYL and CpAKRP (Fig. 5c). Due to papaya’s two-year transformation cycle, we used transformed Arabidopsis to validate the role of CpAKRP. Overexpression of CpYYL and CpAKRP partially rescued the 25% seed abortion phenotype in the heterozygous emb506 and akrp mutants (Fig. 5d, e).

Population genomic analysis of CpYYL
To investigate the evolutionary history of YYL, we analyzed 63 sequenced plant genomes. The YYL gene predates seed plants, with orthologs identified in algae, liverworts, mosses, and ferns, the earliest evolutionary origin of YYL gene can be traced to Chlamydomonas, highlighting the early origin and evolution of YYL (Supplementary Fig. 16a). Examination of YYL across 63 gymnosperm and angiosperm genomes revealed strong conservation, particularly in the ANK repeat domain associated with protein interactions (Supplementary Data 6 and Supplementary Fig. 16b). The CpYYL-X allele demonstrated was confirmed to be functional based on its intact gene structure and complementation test. In contrast, the cpyyl-h allele is a pseudogene, lacking expression due to the absence of the first exon and part of the first intron. Nucleotide diversity (π) for CpYYL-X was 5.26e-05 in cultivated and 8.33e-05 in wild papaya, whereas for cpyyl-h, it was 2.01e-06 in cultivated and 3.48e-06 in the wild papaya (Supplementary Fig. 17a, b), indicating limited diversity.

Furthermore, the Tajima’s D value for CpYYL-X was -1.34 in cultivated and -1.15 in wild papaya, with FST scores ranging from 0 to 0.1 (Supplementary Fig. 17c–f). These values suggest a potential selection pressure acting on this allele. In contrast, cpyyl-h’s Tajima’s D value was near zero (Supplementary Fig. 17f), indicating that this pseudogene has not been subject to selection pressures due to mutations.

Recombination suppression between HSY and MSY in YYh male papaya
The creation of viable YYh male plants offered an unprecedented opportunity to identify the carpel suppressing sex determination gene in male flowers through forward genetics. “SunUp” females were crossed with 24-6 YYh males and generated a testcross population segregating males to hermaphrodites at 1:1 ratio. Male- and hermaphrodite-specific DNA markers were used to genotyping 537 testcross plants (Supplementary Fig. 18), yielding 294 male and 243 hermaphrodite genotypes, perfectly matching the sex phenotypes with zero recombinant plants (Supplementary Data 7).

We also examined the sex segregation ratio in the offspring of the two test cross 20-1 and 15-4 population (Supplementary Figs. 19 and 20). The 20-1 testcross population consisted of 194 plants, with 110 hermaphrodites and 84 males, while the 15-4 testcross population comprised 483 plants, with 236 hermaphrodites and 247 male plants. Both populations fitted to a 1:1 male to hermaphrodite segregation ratio (Chi-square test, p=0.062 for 20–1 populations and p=0.616 for 15–4 populations).
paper_content.methods:
Material and conditions
The papaya seedlings, SunUp, ZH, and AU9 are preserved resources in the Center for Genomics and Biotechnology at Fujian Agriculture and Forestry University, while the Zhongbai variety was purchased from the market. The papaya seedlings were cultivated in the greenhouse at Fujian Agriculture and Forestry University, maintained at a temperature of 28°C with a 16-h light/8-hour dark photoperiod. After two months of cultivation, the seedlings were planted in the papaya field in Yongchun, Fujian, and in the experimental plots within the campus of Fujian Agriculture and Forestry University. Arabidopsis thaliana wild-type ecotype Columbia (Col), along with transgenic and mutant lines, were cultivated in MetroMix 360 soil under controlled conditions of 22°C, 55% relative humidity, and a 16-h light/8-h dark photoperiod.

Generation of transgenic plants
To explore the function of the CpYYL-X copy and to produce viable YhYh genotypes in papaya. We transformed female papaya calli with the construct ProCpYYL_X::CpYYL_X. To construct the vector ProCpYYL_X::CpYYL_X, we utilized the expression vector pOX from our laboratory. The 4.7 kb promoter region and the 990 bp CpYYL_X coding sequence (CDS) fragment were amplified by PCR and subsequently cloned into the pOX vector. The primer sequences (synthesized by Sangon Biotech, Shanghai) were as follows: Pro-CpYYLF: ACCGGAATTCATCGCGACTTGTAGGTGCCATAGT; Pro-CpYYLR: AACCCTGCAGTGATTGCCAACTTGT
TTATTCAACCCTTGTGT; CpYYLCDSF: AAAAACTGCAGATGGCCTCGTGGGCTACGACAGTT; CpYYLCDSR: CCCAACGCGTTTATGGATATTGGTCAGTTGCTATGATC. The genetic transformation procedure was primarily adapted from the protocol previously published43. Specifically, K5 medium containing 5 mg/L 2,4-D and 0.2 mg/L KT was used to induce callus formation (1/2 MS + 5 mg/L 2,4-D + 0.2 mg/L KT + 3 g/L hytagel + 30 g/L sucrose). We used the young hypocotyls of ZH tissue culture seedlings as explants. Subsequently, medium M13 (1/2 MS + 5 mg/L 2,4-D + 3 g/L phytagel + 30 g/L sucrose) was employed to promote embryogenic callus development. In the final stage, embryogenic calli were transferred to CMM (1/2 MS + 10 mg/L 2,4-D + 3 g/L phytagel + 70 g/L sucrose) medium to encourage multiplication. These multiplied embryogenic calli were then subjected to Agrobacterium-mediated transformation. Embryogenic callus induction followed a three-step method, which could significantly improve induction efficiency and shorten the induction period44,45. For the transformation process, papaya embryogenic calli were immersed in transformation buffer for 15 min, and co-cultivation on CMM medium for 24 h. Post co-cultivation, the tissues were transferred to CIM1 medium (1/2 MS + 10 mg/L 2,4-D + 3 g/L phytagel + 70 g/L sucrose) for somatic embryogenesis, with carbenicillin (200 mg/L) and cefotaxime (200 mg/L) treatments. After two weeks, the tissues were moved to selection medium MBN (1/2 MS medium with 0.2 mg/L each of benzylaminopurine (6-BA) and naphthalene acetic acid (NAA), 100 mg/L timentin, and 25 mg/L hygromycin) to select putative transgenic calli. Plantlet regeneration was achieved using MBN for shoot development and IBA rooting medium (1/2 MS with 0.2 mg/L IBA). To verify hygromycin-resistant seedlings, we utilized PCR with two pairs of primers. One pair was designed to amplify the CpYYL coding sequence. The second primer was used to amplify a segment of the CpYYL coding sequence along with the vector sequence.

Genotyping of YhYh and YYh genotype plant
The CpYYL expression vector driven by its native promoter was introduced into ZH female calli to obtain T1 generation plants. These T1 plants were then crossed with hermaphroditic plants, such as SunUp XYh, to generate the F1 population. We initially screened for CpYYL transgenic plants using two pairs of transgene verification primers previously mentioned. Next, the W11 primer was employed to identify male or hermaphroditic plants46. The screened hermaphroditic transgenic plants were subjected to self-pollination. Seeds from these self-pollinations were planted in seed trays, and once the seedlings developed three leaves, PCR identification was conducted to screen for YhYh or YYh plants. Using transgene verification primers and W11 primer, we identified transgenic plants containing Y or Yh copies. The Intron1, PYhCpXYh31-1 and PYhCpXYh31-2 primers target the X copy-specific fragment of CpYYL and PYhCpXYh31. Amplification of three fragments indicate the presence of the X chromosome, while failure to amplify suggests a YhYh or YYh genotype. The TE-1 Yh-specific primer, designed based on the TE upstream of the CpMp gene, successfully amplifies the band in Yh copy, not the Y copy. Conversely, the TE-2 Y-specific primer, positioned at the TE insertion site, amplifies a band exclusively in males, but not in hermaphrodites. These specific primers allow us to distinguish between YhYh and YYh plants.

To further verify the accuracy of YhYh plants, we conducted second-generation resequencing by illumina xplus. Duplicate and low-quality reads were filtered out using Picard tools (v.2.20.4, https://github.com/broadinstitute/picard) and Trimmomatic47 (a Java software, v0.38), respectively. Filtered reads were aligned to SunUp reference with BWA-MEM (v0.7.17-r1188)48, and the SAM output file was converted to the BAM format using the SAMtools suite49. The BAM files were visualized using IGV-GSAman (v.0.8.8) (https://gitee.com/CJchen/IGV-sRNA). By evaluating 15 high-confidence SNP markers located in the MSY and HSY region, we confirmed the YhYh genotype. Additionally, we assessed the read coverage in the X-specific region. YhYh genotype plants showed very low coverage compared to the XYh control, indicating the absence of the X copy in the verified YhYh genotype plants. Through molecular and sequencing validation, we successfully identified YhYh plants.

Design and preparation of Y-chromosome-specific oligoprobe
We used an established methodology to identify Y-chromosome-specific oligonucleotides50 within the SunUp genome2. The oligonucleotides were screened using Chorus2 software51, with the detailed protocol outlined as follows: oligonucleotides (59 nucleotides in length) unique to the SunUp genome, employing a step size of 5 nucleotides. Oligonucleotides were excluded if they mapped to multiple locations with at least 75% similarity across the genome. We chose oligonucleotides with a differential melting temperature (dTm) greater than 10°C, where dTm is defined as the melting temperature minus the hairpin melting temperature. Genomic sequenced data from SunUp was used to filter out potential repeats. Ultimately, 2499 Y-chromosome-specific oligonucleotides were selected from a 3.2 Mb region, spanning positions 0.9–4.1 Mb on the Y-chromosome, and the library was synthesized by MYcroarray (Ann Arbor, MI, USA)

The preparation of oligonucleotide probes followed the previously described protocol50. Briefly, the library underwent PCR amplification to produce a double-stranded DNA template, which was subsequently transcribed into RNA. The library was labeled through reverse transcription of the RNA using a 5′ biotin-labeled primer. Unincorporated primers and the RNA template were degraded to yield a labeled, single-stranded oligonucleotide probe.

Preparation of chromosome spreads and fluorescence in situ hybridization
Chromosome preparation followed a previously established protocol50. In brief, root tips were harvested from potted plants and pre-treated with 2 mM 8-hydroxyquinoline at 25°C for 2 h. Subsequently, the root tips were fixed overnight in a 3:1 (v/v) ethanol:glacial acetic acid solution at 25°C. After a brief rinse in distilled water, the root tips were incubated in an enzymatic solution containing 2% cellulase Onozuka-R10 (Yakult Pharmaceutical, Tokyo, Japan) and 1% pectolyase from Aspergillus niger (Sigma-Aldrich Corp., St. Louis, MO, USA). Following another rinse in distilled water, the root tips were fixed again in the ethanol:acetic acid (3:1) solution. Cells were dissociated by gently breaking the root tips with a pipette tip, and the resulting cell suspension was applied to glass slides. The slides were air-dried and stored at −20°C until further use.

FISH was performed as previously described in “Method”52. The procedure is that hybridization signals were visualized using Alexa Fluor 488 streptavidin at a dilution of 1:100 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) for biotin-labeled probes and rhodamine-conjugated anti-digoxigenin at a dilution of 1:200 (Roche Diagnostics, Basel, Switzerland) for digoxigenin-labeled probes. Chromosomes were counterstained with DAPI (2 mg/mL) and mounted in Vectashield (Vector). Metaphase plates with fluorescent signals were observed using an Olympus BX63 fluorescent microscope, photographed with an Olympus DP80 CCD camera, and analyzed with cellSens Dimension 1.9 software (Olympus Corporation, Tokyo, Japan).

Phenotypic observation of the pollen from YYh, ZH XY, and AU9 XY flowers
We collected fresh pollen from ZH YYh, AU9 YYh, and AU9 XY flowers, selecting those that had just bloomed for their active and easily collectible pollen. The pollen was carefully extracted and evenly distributed onto a microscope slide to ensure uniform observation. The pollen was added 2–3 drops of Alexander stain, and then covered with a coverslip to prevent evaporation and ensure even staining. After 5 h of staining, the slide was photographed with a microscope Axioimage A2 1701943S (Carl Zeiss, Oberkochen, Germany) to observe the stained pollen’s shape, size, and surface features. For a detailed structural and morphological analysis of pollen, we securely placed fresh pollen onto a slide with double-sided tape and observed it using a Hitachi TM3030 PLUS scanning electron microscope (SEM) (Hitachi, Tokyo, Japan).

Paraffin section and hybridization in situ
For paraffin section analysis, seeds of Zhongbai papaya variety were collected at 35, 42, 49, 65, 72, and 79 DAP and fixed in FAA (formaldehyde–acetic acid–ethanol) solution. The samples underwent dehydration through a graded ethanol series, followed by treatment with ethanol and xylene solutions for clearing. Subsequently, the samples were infiltrated with paraffin wax, embedded, and sectioned at a thickness of 8 μm using a Leica RM2235 microtome. Sections were stained with a 1% hematoxylin-eosin solution (dissolved in 95% ethanol) for 30 min. After staining, 1–2 drops of mounting medium were applied to the glass slide. Observations were made under microscope Axioimage A2 1701943S (Carl Zeiss, Oberkochen, Germany). The above methods were referenced from literature and modified accordingly53.

For hybridization in situ, hermaphrodite ovules of the Zhongbai cultivar were harvested at 35, 50, 65, 75, 85, and 115 DAP and prepared for paraffin sectioning as previously described54. The dehydrated samples were embedded in paraffin and sectioned at 8 μm.

Probe preparation followed kit instructions (Roche DIG RNA labeling kit SP6/T7), with T7 promoter sequences added as a 5’-tail on the reverse primer for probe region amplification (pCRII-TOPO, Invitrogen). Target DNA was reverse-transcribed to mRNA using a DIG-UTP labeling kit (Roche DIG RNA labeling kit SP6/T7), and probe length was reduced to 150 bp by fragmentation.

Tissue sections were deparaffinized and rehydrated through a graded ethanol series. Acetic anhydride solution was prepared immediately before use, and protease was added at the time of use. Hybridization probes were used at a final concentration of 0.5 ng/μl probe complexity. For hybridizations performed with 100 μl per slide, approximately 25 ng of probe was used per slide for 0.5-kb probes and 50 ng per slide for 1-kb probes. Slides were incubated at 55°C for 16–20 h. Following hybridization, slides were incubated with anti-digoxigenin antibody diluted in washing buffer (1:5 v/v) in the dark for 2–3 h at room temperature or overnight at 4°C. Sections were photographed by using NI-U research grade upright microscope (Nikon Corporation, Tokyo, Japan).

RNA-seq analysis
The paired-end RNA-seq sequences were generated using the Illumina xplus sequencing platform. Initially, quality control was performed using Fastp55 to ensure high-quality sequences. The clean reads were then aligned to the papaya reference genome2 using HISAT2 (v.2.2.1)56, a fast and sensitive alignment tool. The alignment results, initially in SAM format, were sorted and converted into BAM format using Samtools (v.1.19)57 for efficient storage and processing.

Subsequently, FeatureCounts58 was employed to quantify gene expression by counting the reads mapped to genomic features. Differential expression analysis was conducted using DESeq2 (v.1.42.0)59, with criteria set to LogFC>1 and Padj<0.05, to identify DEGs. To explore the functional implications of the DEGs, NR annotations were utilized, and GO enrichment and KEGG enrichment were conducted using the OmicShare online platform. These analyses provided insights into the biological processes and functional capabilities of the genes across different conditions.

Subcellular localization assays
The open reading frames (ORFs) of full-length CpYYL-X, and CpYYL-X-2F (remove signal peptide of CpYYL-X, residues were from 111 to 329) were inserted into the pMDC202-GFP vector to produce the pMDC202-CpYYL-X-GFP and pMDC202-CpYYL-X-2F-GFP recombinant expression vectors, then they were separately introduced into Agrobacterium tumefaciens strain GV3101 using the freeze-thaw method60. Nicotiana benthamiana leaves were prepared for transient transformation via leaf infiltration with a solution of Agrobacterium cells. After 48 h, GFP fluorescence signals were observed under a confocal laser-scanning microscope (SP8X, Leica, Germany).

Bimolecular fluorescence complementation assay
The full-length coding sequence of CpYYL or CpAKRP without the stop codon was cloned into the vector SPYNE to generate p35S CpYYL/CpAKRP-YFPN vector. The full-length coding sequences of CpYYL and CpAKRP were cloned into the vector SPYCE by In-Fusion cloning to generate p35S CpYYL/CpAKRP-YFPC vector, respectively, by using a ClonExpress Ultra One Step Cloning Kit (Vazyme Biotech Co., Ltd). The different combinations of YFPN and YFPC fusion vectors were coinfiltrated into tobacco leaf epidermal cells. Agrobacterium tumefaciens strain GV3101 cells harboring the above different constructs were cultured to OD600=0.8, then centrifuged, and the pellet was resuspended in infiltration buffer (1 mM methyl ester sulfonate, 10 mM MgCl2, and 150 mM acetosyringone, pH 5.7). Different combinations of vectors were mixed equally and coinfiltrated into leaves from 3-week-old Nicotiana benthamiana. Then they were used to detect the signal of reconstituted YFP fluorescence by a confocal laser-scanning microscope (SP8X, Leica, Germany) in the dark for 48 h after infiltration61.

RNA extraction and quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR)
In order to analyze the expression of genes, total RNA was extracted using the RNA Isolation Kit (TAKARA). The reverse transcription of total RNA was performed with PrimeScript TM RT reagent Kit, which includes gDNA Eraser (TAKARA). qPCR was conducted using TB Green SYBR Premix Ex Taq TM II (Tli RNaseH Plus) (TAKARA). qPCR was carried out using a CFX real-time PCR system (BioRad). Data from three biological replicates were used to calculate expression levels using the 2−△△CT method62. CpActin was used to normalize the RNA levels between different samples. Analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to test the significance of expression level. Three technical replicates for each sample were performed for qPCR analysis.

Yeast screening assay
For pGBKT7 (Clontech) bait vectors, the truncated coding sequences of CpYYL were fused down-stream of the GAL4 DNA binding domain (BD). The cDNA library of the papaya samples from flower, leaf and immature fruit was constructed using a Gateway approach by Ouyi Company. Two-Hybrid Library Screening is using Yeast Mating utilizing the natural ability of haploid yeast strains as Y187 and Y2H Gold to mate with each other to form a diploid cell. Spread the mated culture on the triple dropout supplements (TDO) plates. High stringency patching to identify potential binding partners on the quadruple dropout supplements (QDO) plates (Clontech). Positive cloned yeast plasmids were extracted and sequenced. After sequencing the positive clones, the sequence results were blasted by NCBI and got to the target sequence. Then, Yeast Two-Hybrid was chosen to further confirm each screening protein–protein interaction.

Yeast two-hybrid assay
For pGBKT7 (Clontech) bait vectors, the truncated coding sequences of CpYYL were fused downstream of the GAL4 DNA-binding domain to generate the BD recombinant plasmid. For pGADT7 (Clontech) prey vectors, the full-length coding sequences of CpAKRP were fused to downstream of the GAL4 activation domain to generate AD recombinant plasmid. Different combinations of BD and AD constructs were co-transformed into the yeast strain Y2HGOLD using a Frozen-EZ Yeast Transformation II Kit (MKbio). The manipulations were performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Clontech) and previous studies63. The interaction between pGBKT7-53 (Human P53) and pGADT7-T (T-antigen) was used as a positive control. The interactions between pGADT7-empty and pGBKT7-empty were used as a negative control. Co-transformants were subsequently spotted on SD/-Leu/-Trp medium (DDO) and to assess protein interactions, the positive yeast clones were spotted onto SD/-Ade/-His/-Leu/-Trp medium (QDO) with a series of dilution concentrations. The Interactions results were observed after incubation at 30°C after 3 days.

Arabidopsis genetic transformation analysis
The emb506 (SALK_054289C) T-DNA insertion mutant was sourced from Arashare, while the akrp (CS16042, CS26041) T-DNA insertion mutant was generously provided by Lixin Zhang’s lab at Henan University. Plasmid constructs were generated using the ClonExpress II One Step Cloning Kit (Vazyme). For transgenic plant generation, the cDNA of CpYYL was inserted into the XbaI and SalI sites of the pMDC202 vector, and the cDNA of CpAKRP was inserted into the XhoI and SalI sites of the pGWB505 vector. These constructs were subsequently introduced into Agrobacterium tumefaciens strain GV3101.

Heterozygous seeds of emb506 and akrp mutants were cultivated to flowering, after which the overexpression constructs were introduced via the floral dip method64. Transgenic plants were selected on 1/2 MS medium supplemented with 30 µg/mL hygromycin and 50 µg/mL kanamycin. Successful integration of the transgenes in the T1 generation was confirmed by PCR. Homozygous transgenic lines were identified in the T3 generation, and two lines were selected for further analysis. For each line, at least 30 siliques were harvested to assess sterility rates.

GC-MS analysis of sugars
Freeze-dried papaya ovules from both female and hermaphroditic plants at 15, 35, and 65 days DAP (total 16 samples) were pulverized using a mixer mill (MM400, Retsch) equipped with a zirconia bead, operating at 30 Hz for 1.5 min, three biological replicates were performed. A 20 mg portion of the resulting powder was diluted to 500 μL with a methanol:isopropanol:water mixture (3:3:2, v/v/v), followed by vortexing for 3 min and sonication for 30 min. A 50 μL aliquot of the supernatant was combined with 20 μL of an internal standard solution (ribitol, 1000 μg/mL) and evaporated under a nitrogen gas stream. The dried sample was then subjected to freeze-drying using a lyophilizer, and the residue was prepared for derivatization.

For derivatization, the sample was treated with 100 μL of methoxyamine hydrochloride in pyridine (15 mg/mL) and incubated at 37°C for 2 h. Subsequently, 100 μL of BSTFA was added, and the mixture was vortexed and maintained at 37°C for an additional 30 min. The derivatized sample was then diluted to an appropriate concentration for GC-MS analysis.

GC-MS analysis was performed using an Agilent 8890 gas chromatograph coupled to a 5977B mass spectrometer, equipped with a DB-5MS column (30 m length × 0.25 mm i.d. × 0.25 μm film thickness, J&W Scientific, USA). Helium was used as the carrier gas at a flow rate of 1 mL/min. Samples were injected in split mode with a split ratio of 5:1, and an injection volume of 1 μL. The oven temperature program was as follows initial hold at 170°C for 2 minutes, ramp to 240°C at 10°C/min, further increase to 280°C at 5°C/min, and a final increase to 310°C at 25°C/min, with a hold for 4 min. All analyses were conducted in selective ion monitoring mode, with the ion source and transfer line temperatures set at 230°C and 240°C, respectively65,66. Sugar contents were quantified by MetWare (http://www.metware.cn/) using the Agilent 8890-5977B platform.

Statistical analysis was conducted in the R environment, with differentially accumulated metabolites screened using a Fold Change|≥2 threshold, and pathway enrichment analysis performed using a one-tailed hypergeometric test.

Multiple sequence alignment and tree construction
Sequences of EMB506 proteins, annotated from transcripts and genomes, were aligned using MUSCLE (v.5.1)67 with default parameters. The regions poorly aligned were trimmed using trimAl (v.1.4)68 and the trimmed alignments were used for the construction of a maximum likelihood tree using IQ-TREE (v.2.1.4)69 under the optimal substitution model. For each tree, 1000 replicates were conducted to generate bootstrap values. The trees were viewed using iTOL (v6)70, while Jalview was utilized for viewing the alignment results.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In the present manuscript, the genes and genomic architecture in the sex-determining regions (SDRs) that control sex segregation and characteristics of each sex were identified in papaya. Particularly, it is noteworthy that the authors succeeded in identifying the gene responsible for lethality in Y or Yh homozygotes and the successful production of Y (Yh) homozygous individuals by complementation with overexpression of the causal gene. Also, it was novel and unique works that mutants showing the sex reversal phenotype were screened and identified. Each study was excellent and quite informative for elucidating structure and functions of papaya sex chromosomal regions.
Although there are multiple unique and novel discoveries and efforts made in this study, first, the objective of the study in this paper is not clearly stated. According to the results in this paper, multiple targets for the studies seem to be present in this study. Of course, they are related to sex chromosome (Y, Yh) in papaya, but I could not understand the identity of the study in this paper. Owing to this, it was impressed that identified findings shown in the result section were quite dispersed.
Regarding to each specific result,
Firstly, I could not find how the CpEMB506 gene was identified or regarded is as the candidate for YY lethality gene in papaya? Furthermore, the X allele of CpEMB506 is described as functional allele, but its evidences were not shown in this study. The result that YhYh individuals were successfully developed in the CpEMB506-OX progeny is the quite impressive and novel result, but there seems to be no detail of their phenotypes.
On the other hand, whole genome sequencing of transgenic individuals of CpEMB506 (CpYYL)-OX plants was performed to determine the position of transgene insertions, but I am not sure how these results contribute to the main story or objectives in this paper.
YhYh and YYh plants derived from CpEMB506-OX individuals are certainly helpful for determining the HSY and MSY sequences and finding their structural differences systematically, but it is not always worth enumerating each structural variations in p7, because further analyses of these variations were not carried out in this paper.
Next, it is also unclear why the authors focused on CpMp gene in this study. It seems that the functional elucidation of CpMp will be shown in another publication, but its citation seems to be shown, but it was insufficient (no statement on publication status). Since the details of the revised article for CpMp gene study were unknown, I am not sure if there is any overlap with the data and description presented in this paper. It was essential for authors to discriminate the results and experimental data between present paper and another manuscript under review for avoiding replicate or duplicate publications.
Obtained sex reversal mutants must be quite useful materials for identifying genes and elucidating the mechanism of papaya sex determination. But, it seemed to be waste of these sex reversal mutants to demonstrate that CpMp gene was not likely to be the candidate genes for sex determination. Is it necessary for this study??
Again, topic of CpYYL appeared in the latter part of results section without any continuity to previous descriptions, so it should be described in an organized manner.
In the discussion, related to the title of this paper, definition or meaning of “domestication” in papaya should be well considered.
I suppose that the domestication of papaya (Carica papaya) is the emergence of trioecy (hermaphrodite), and/or increased fruit size in hermaphrodite in comparison with female fruit. The YY lethality by CPYYL gene as described in this paper was suggested to contribute to the establishment of dioecy in the papaya (or its ancestors) before domestication. CpMp is suggested to be the gene for peduncles length. Though there are differences in peduncle length between male and hermaphrodite plants, I am not sure how change of peduncle length affects the domestication of papaya.
As the additional issues,
YY, YhYh, and YYh lethality should be considered as the same phenomena? So far as present manuscript, these words seemed to be co-existed in the text.
In discussion, what does "super hermaphrodite YhYh plant" mean in its phenotype?
In Fig4k, show pictures of female flowers rather than female fruits.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
The manuscript "Recreating viable YhYh genotype uncovers a domestication event of the Yh chromosome in papaya" presents a groundbreaking study on the domestication and genetic basis of sex determination in papaya with a focus on the Y chromosome. Key findings include the identification of the YY lethality gene (CpYYL) and its role in embryo viablity as well as the discovery of a retrotransposon insertion in the CpMp-h promoter as a crucial domestication event. Moreover, the authors successfully generated viable YhYh and YYh genotypes, addressing a long-standing challenge in papaya breeding. Although papaya is not a classical easily manipulated lab model, the authors provide strong functional validation of the genes studied. The figures effectively illustrate key results, such as FISH validation, structural variants, and methylation patterns.
However, the manuscript is dense particularly in the Results section. Reorganizing for better readability — such as adding subheadings or including a summary figure of the experimental workflow — would be helpful.
Some terms (e.g., "stage 3 sex chromosomes") are introduced without sufficient context for non-specialists.
The partial lethality of YhYh/YYh genotypes (59.6% and 26.9% mortality) is attributed to missing X-specific genes but lacks mechanistic detail. It would be beneficial to discuss whether this lethality results from haploinsufficiency or specific gene interactions.
For improved clarity, adding a schematic model summarizing the molecular mechanism of YY lethality, CpYYL function, and the domestication of Yh is recommended.
Despite these comments, the manuscript represents a significant contribution to understanding the evolution and domestication of papaya, and I recommend it for acceptance after revisions.

Response: Thank you very much for your assessment and suggestions. The objectives of this
study are to identify the gene controlling YY lethality and to restore viable YhYh hermaphrodite
for breeding true breeding hermaphrodite cultivars to solve the long-standing problem of sex
segregating seedlings. We have identified and validated the X-specific gene CpYYL controlling
YY lethality, and created viable YhYh hermaphrodites, which are being used in our papaya
breeding program. We have added these two objectives at the end of the introduction section.
In the process of assembling and analyzing the haplotype resolved YYh genome, we
identified a retrotransposon insertion in the promoter region of the long male peduncle gene,
CpMp, which led to the reversion of the long male peduncles into short hermaphrodite peduncles
in papaya. This event plays a crucial role in the domestication of hermaphrodite papaya from a
dioecious population in Central America about 4,000 years ago.
However, this finding is not relevant to our objectives in this study. As per your suggestion,
although each finding is significant, the presence of multiple research outcomes made the paper
appear less focused. Therefore, we have restructured the manuscript to focus primarily on the in-
depth analysis of the CpYYL gene function. We have removed the sections on the CpMp gene and
the sex-reversal mutants to focus on the study's main objectives.
Regarding to each specific result, firstly, I could not find how the CpEMB506 gene was identified
or regarded is as the candidate for YY lethality gene in papaya?
Response: We have added how we identified the candidate gene and revised relevant text as
below:
1
“Given the lethal phenotype observed in YY/YhYh individuals, we hypothesize that the gene
responsible for YhYh lethality remains functional in the X chromosome but becomes non-
functional in the MSY. To investigate this, we screened for X/Y gene/pseudogene pairs located in
the MSY and its X counterpart, focusing on those implicated in embryonic development. This
analysis identified CpEMB506, an X- specific gene with a Y-pseudogene allele. Its ortholog in
Arabidopsis is associated with embryo abortion16, making CpEMB506 as a strong candidate gene
underlying YhYh lethality. The X allele features a large first intron of 8374 bp, which includes
DNA transposons and LTR retrotransposons. In contrast, the HSY allele has lost the first exon
(409 bp) and 7352 bp in the first intron, rendering it a pseudogene (Fig. 2a and b). A comparison
of the coding DNA sequences of X, HSY, and MSY alleles revealed that the disrupted MSY and
HSY alleles share conserved sequences, but differ from the X allele by SNPs and Indels
(Supplementary Fig. 3).”
References
Albert, S., Després, B., Guilleminot, J., Bechtold, N., Pelletier, G., Delseny, M., and Devic, M.
(1999). The EMB 506 gene encodes a novel ankyrin repeat containing protein that is
essential for the normal development of Arabidopsis embryos. Plant J 17, 169-179.
Wang, J., Na, J.K., Yu, Q., Gschwend, A.R., Han, J., Zeng, F., Aryal, R., Vanburen, R.,
Murray, J.E., and Zhang, W. (2012). Sequencing papaya X and Yh chromosomes

109, 13710-13715.

rescued the embryonic lethal phenotype of the YhYh genotype, enabling YhYh individuals to
survive (Fig.2c-h). This complementation provides the most direct and compelling evidence that
the X allele is functional, as the CpEMB506_X protein can support normal embryonic
development. Consistent with this, the X allele encodes a complete protein with intact functional
domains , whereas the Yh allele is predicted to produce a truncated protein (Fig.2a-b). Moreover,
the normal presence of the X allele in female XX plants and their fertility further corroborate its
functional role.

plants. Now that the YhYh plants have flowered, we confirmed that they produce normal
hermaphroditic flowers (Fig.2d-h). Pollen viability assays showed that YhYh plants have
comparable pollen viability to XYh plants (Supplementary Fig.12b-c). Plant height and flower
2
length also did not differ significantly between the two genotypes (Fig. 2i and Supplementary
Fig.12a). These results indicate that the surviving YhYh plants exhibit normal growth,
development, and fertility to XYh plants.
On the other hand, whole genome sequencing of transgenic individuals of CpEMB506 (CpYYL)-
OX plants was performed to determine the position of transgene insertions, but I am not sure how
these results contribute to the main story or objectives in this paper.

genome sequencing on transgenic CpYYL plants to investigate whether of transgene insertion sites
influenced the ability to obtain viable YhYh progeny. While some transgenic lines successfully
produced viable YhYh individuals, others did not. Our analysis showed that the four insertion sites
were located in intergenic regions, with only one event within a gene, which did not affect its
expression. We found no evidence that the viability of YhYh is directly linked to the transgene
insertion sitesBecause these findings do not contribute to the primary focus of the CpEMB506
functional study, we decided to remove this section to maintain a clear and focused narrative.

determining the HSY and MSY sequences and finding their structural differences systematically,
but it is not always worth enumerating each structural variations in p7, because further analyses of
these variations were not carried out in this paper.

We ensure that there is no data overlap between these two studies. During haplotype

controlling long male peduncles in papaya.

Response: The CpMp gene is a critical sex-determining factor, known as the male peduncle,
responsible for the long, ramified, many-flowered cymose inflorescence of male trees (Storey,
1953). The emergence of hermaphroditic flowers is a pivotal event in papaya domestication
(Vanburen et al., 2015), yet alterations in peduncle length may represent an adaptive trait that
evolved concurrently with domestication. The retention of long peduncles in male flowers is
primarily advantageous for increasing pollen production and enhancing pollen dispersal.
Conversely, when male flowers are domesticated into hermaphroditic flowers, long peduncles can
pose a challenge by increasing the distance required for nutrient transport. Previous studies have
shown that the structural properties significantly influence fruit pedicel (FP) traits such as length,
weight, and diameter, directly contributing to the development of high-quality fruits in cucumber
(Che and Zhang, 2019). Fruit deformation can occur when the pedicel is excessively long or too
short (Yane et al., 2024). Additionally, shorter, sturdier peduncles may offer better support for
developing hermaphroditic fruits, mitigating the risk of fruit drop due to gravity or adverse
weather conditions like wind and rain. Consequently, under the continuous selective pressure
exerted by humans for high-yield, large-fruited hermaphroditic plants, individuals with relatively
shorter peduncles may gain an advantage in the efficiency of assimilate transport to the fruit,
leading to their indirect selection and eventual fixation. The variations in peduncle length
regulated by the CpMp gene may illustrate how papaya has optimized resource allocation and
reproductive strategies for different sexes during domestication, with male flowers focusing on
efficient pollination and hermaphroditic flowers on efficient fruiting.

## Abstract

Papaya is a trioecious species with XX females, XY males, and XYh hermaphrodites. Any combination of Y and Yh chromosomes is lethal. The gene underlying YY lethality is pivotal in the transition from stage 2 to stage 3 in sex chromosome evolution. Here, we identify and functionally validate the YY lethality gene in papaya, CpYYL. Loss of CpYYL function accelerates glycolysis and reduces sucrose accumulation in embryo, causing embryo abortion. CpYYL interacts with CpAKRP and overexpression of both genes partially rescues seed abortion in the heterozygous emb506 and akrp mutants, indicating conserved role in plastid differentiation and embryo development. Viable YYh and YhYh plants are generated through genetic engineering and crossing, although both genotypes show high seedling mortality. Crossing YYh male with XX female papaya shows 1:1 ratio of male to hermaphrodite plants without recombination between MSY and HSY. Identification of CpYYL fills a critical gap in papaya sex chromosome evolution, and provides new resources for genomic and epigenetic studies.

---

## Introduction

Papaya (Carica papaya L., 2n=2x=18) is a fast-growing fruit crop known for its palatable flavor, rich nutritional profile, and versatile culinary and medicinal applications. It is native to Central America and southern Mexico and is now cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions worldwide. The papaya fruit is a large, fleshy berry that varies in size, shape, and color depending on the variety. Papaya pulp is rich in provitamin A, vitamin C, and other essential nutrients, making it a popular choice for fresh consumption and processed products like juices, jams, and dried fruit. The protease enzyme papain is widely used in the food, pharmaceutical, and cosmetic industries. Papaya has been recommended as a dietary intervention to prevent vitamin A deficiency in developing countries1.

Papaya is a diploid species with 9 chromosomes and a genome size of 352Mb2. Transgenic papaya has been widely publicized as a success story that saved the papaya industry from an epidemic of papaya ringspot virus (PRSV)3,4. Since the devastating PRSV disease has been effectively controlled, the primary problem for papaya production is the segregation of sex types. In most papaya-producing regions, hermaphrodites are preferred due to their higher productivity and compact, pear-shaped fruits, which reduce shipping costs by 20%. However, the progeny from self-fertilized hermaphrodites segregate in a 2:1 ratio (two hermaphrodites to one female), while progeny from female trees pollinated by hermaphrodites segregate in a 1:1 ratio (one hermaphrodite to one female). This occurs because YhYh embryos are nonviable. Farmers relying on hermaphrodites for production need to plant at least five seedlings per planting hill and wait 4–6 months until flowering. Thinning is then performed to maximize the number of hermaphrodite plants. This practice is labor-intensive and inefficient, resulting in wasted time, water, and nutrients while delaying production due to competition among the plants in early growth. This has been a problem since the beginning of papaya cultivation that persists to this day5. Identifying the gene responsible for YY lethality could pave the way for engineering viable YYh and YhYh genotypes. These genotypes are essential germplasms for developing true-breeding hermaphrodite cultivars by crossing XX females with YhYh hermaphrodites.

Dioecy and sex chromosomes are common in animals but rare in plants, occurring in approximately 10% land plant species and 6% of flowering plant species6,7. The evolution of sex chromosomes can be categorized into six stages. Stage 3 involves the expansion of the male-specific region due to the accumulation of retrotransposons, translocation and duplication of genomic fragments. This process is accompanied by Y chromosome degeneration, resulting in the lethality of the YY genotype. Consequently, males are restricted to the heterozygous XY genotype, as observed in papaya6.

Cultivated hermaphrodite papaya was selected from a male population in Central America about 4000 years ago, resulting in a modified Yh chromosome8. The male- and hermaphrodite-specific region of the Y and Yh chromosomes (MSY and HSY) has been sequenced9. The identity of MSY and HSY is 99.6%, indicating they share a common ancestral MSY recently8.

Extensively studied plant sex chromosomes include those of white campion (Silene latifolia Poir.)10–12, papaya8,9, and asparagus (Asparagus officinalis L.)13,14. The successful assembly of the asparagus YY genome led to the identification of two sex determination genes in the asparagus MSY14. A major challenge in studying MSY in papaya and white campion is the unavailability of YY genotype. In the XY genotype, the X chromosome does not recombine with MSY, rendering genes in MSY genetically unmappable15,16. This limitation could be overcome if viable YY genotypes of papaya could be recreated.

Classical genetic analyses led to the hypothesis of five factors in the sex determination region, contributing to distinctive morphologies among the three sex types in papaya17. 1. Mp, male peduncle, responsible for the long, ramified, many-flowered cymose inflorescence of male trees; 2. l, zygotic lethal (i.e., YY lethality); 3. sa, suppressor of the androecium; 4. sg, suppressor of the gynoecium; 5. C, hypothetical factor for recombination suppression in the sex determining region. We have discovered that the factor C is two inversions that occurred 7 and 1.9 million years ago (mya), respectively9. Together, these five factors—four genes and two chromosomal rearrangements—are essential for papaya sex chromosomes to reach stage 3, characterized by YY lethality. The objectives of this study are to identify the YY lethality gene and generate viable YhYh hermaphrodites for papaya improvement.

In this work, we identify CpYYL as the gene responsible for YY lethality in papaya, a defining feature of its evolved sex chromosomes. Using transgenic complementation, we generate viable YYh and YhYh plants, providing critical resources for dissecting sex chromosome recombination. We further demonstrate that CpYYL interacts with CpAKRP and that loss of CpYYL disrupts sucrose metabolism, leading to embryo abortion. These findings directly link the degeneration of an essential gene on the Y chromosome to the stabilization of dioecy, offering evolutionary insights and valuable germplasm for papaya genetic studies and crop improvement.

---

## Results

Identification of a candidate gene controlling YY lethality
Papaya has three sex genotypes: female (XX), hermaphrodite (XYh) and male (XY), each exhibiting distinct floral features (Fig. 1a–c). Self-pollinated hermaphrodite flowers showed a segregation ratio of 2 XYh hermaphrodites to 1 XX female, with ~25% of seeds aborted due to YhYh lethality, lacking discernible embryos (Fig. 1d, e). The aborted YhYh genotype seeds had no discernible embryos (Fig. 1f,g). In contrast, fertilizing female flowers with hermaphrodite pollen resulted in a 1 XYh hermaphrodite to 1 XX female ratio without seed abortion (Fig. 1d, e and Supplementary Table 1).

Papaya ovules exhibited retrograde development, with early and late globular embryos forming at 35 and 49 days post-pollination, respectively. Heart embryos at 65 days, followed by torpedo stage at 72 days, and cotyledon stage at 79 days (Supplementary Fig. 1). However, aborted embryos of the YhYh genotype exhibited phenotypic differences from their normal counterparts. Up to 50 days after pollination (DAP), embryos of the YhYh genotype were indistinguishable from normal XYh embryos. However, as wild-type embryos progressed to the cotyledon stage, YhYh embryos exhibited degeneration of embryo and endosperm (Fig. 1f–i).

Given the lethal phenotype observed in YY/YhYh individuals, we hypothesize that the gene responsible for YY/YhYh lethality remains functional in the X chromosome but becomes non-functional in the MSY and HSY. To investigate this, we screened 34 X-specific genes9 (Supplementary Data 1). Functional annotation identified PYhCpXYh7 encodes an ankyrin repeat domain-containing protein orthologous to Arabidopsis EMB506, which is an essential gene for normal embryo development18. Transcriptomic analysis revealed CpEMB506 is highly expressed across four embryonic stages, with its expression level gradually declining as development proceeds (Supplementary Data 1). The gene function and expression pattern made CpEMB506 as a strong candidate gene underlying YY, YYh, and YhYh lethality. The X allele features a large first intron of 8374 bp, which includes DNA transposons and LTR retrotransposons. In contrast, the HSY allele has lost the first exon (409 bp) and 7352 bp in the first intron, rendering it a pseudogene (Fig. 2a, b). A comparison of the coding DNA sequences of X, HSY, and MSY alleles revealed that the disrupted MSY and HSY alleles share conserved sequences, but differ from the X allele by SNPs and Indels (Supplementary Fig. 2). Further quantitative PCR and RNA-seq data showed that the CpEMB506-X allele is expressed in both embryos and female flowers, whereas Cpemb506-HSY pseudogene is not expressed (Supplementary Fig. 3).

Validation of CpEMB506 function and generation of viable YhYh and YYh papaya plants
To validate the function of CpEMB506, we generated transgenic plants expressing CpEMB506 under its native promoter to assess its ability to rescue the abortion phenotype in YhYh seeds. The pOX vector was transformed into papaya cultivar “Zhonghuang” (ZH) calli using an efficient genetic transformation system (Supplementary Fig. 4). Transgenic lines of ProCpEMB506::CpEMB506/ZH (CpEMB506Pro/ZH) female plants were generated and confirmed via PCR (Supplementary Fig. 5).

These transgenic females were crossed with pollen from hermaphrodite cultivars pollen, producing hermaphrodite F1 plants named transCpEMB506 XYh (ProCpEMB506::CpEMB506/F1 XYh). These F1 plants were then self-pollinated to produce a segregating F2 population, which was subsequently screened to identify YhYh genotype plants (Supplementary Fig. 6). All F2 seeds exhibited black seeds, with no presence of white aborted seeds. In contrast, the control hermaphrodite seeds showed aborted white seeds, indicating that the phenotype of aborted seeds in hermaphroditic plants was partially restored (Fig. 2c). YYh genotype was obtained by crossing CpEMB506Pro/ZH XYh with ZH XY or AU9 XY male plants (Supplementary Fig. 7).

Next, two F2 populations were developed from two test crosses for identifying YhYh and YYh genotype plants, 20–1 population derived from a cross between a “SunUp” female and a 20-1 YYh male, and 15–4 population derived from a cross between a ZH female and a 15-4 YYh male. We identified 94 YYh seedlings from 20–1 population, and 32 YYh from 15–4 population after testing 4652 and 1386 F2 individuals, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 8 and Supplementary Data 2). However, only 18 YhYh plants were identified in the 20–1 population, with no such individuals detected in the 15–4 population (Supplementary Fig. 8 and Supplementary Data 2). All YYh and YhYh were identified using the developed sex-specific CpEMB506, PYhCpXYh31 and TE markers. These markers effectively distinguish between female and hermaphrodite plants, as well as between male and hermaphrodite plants (Supplementary Tables 2 and 3). To further validate the accuracy of the YhYh genotype, we conducted next-generation resequencing on six YhYh plants and eight YYh as control. Sequencing results confirmed the absence of the X-linked sex determination region in all assayed plants (Fig. 2d). We aligned the sequencing data to the AU9 MSY genome as the reference and analyzed 15 high-confidence SNP markers located within the MSY. Genotype analysis revealed that all six YhYh samples matched the HSY genotype, verifying the accuracy of YhYh genotype identification (Supplementary Figs. 9, 10 and Supplementary Data 3). However, all 18 YhYh seedlings and 32 of the 126 YYh seedlings displayed reduced viability, with post-embryonic developmental arrest occurring in 100% of YhYh and 25.4% of YYh individuals (Supplementary Data 2). We observed that the apex of 18 YhYh and 32 YYh seedlings gradually ceased development, leaving only the stem, and eventually, the seedlings died after approximately 10 days of growth (Fig. 2e).

The YYh genotype plants exhibited a male phenotype. Comparative analysis of YYh and XY male plants showed no significant differences in plant height, flower structure, and peduncle length compared to XY males (two-tailed t-test, p=0.14–0.97) (Fig. 2f–i and Supplementary Fig. 11). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) confirmed that pollen morphology and vitality were identical between YYh and XY male flowers (Supplementary Fig. 12).

FISH analysis revealed that the Y-chromosome-specific probe generated one strong signal in one Yh chromosome in XYh hermaphrodite “SunUp”, and two strong signals in two YYh individuals, confirming that the fertility of YYh was restored (Fig. 2j to l). These results validated that CpEMB506 is the gene controlling YY, YYh, YhYh lethality. We renamed this YY lethality gene CpEMB506 as CpYYL.

The CpYYL is expressed in embryo and encodes a chloroplast localized protein
To elucidate the physiological function of CpYYL, its expression was examined across various papaya tissues. CpYYL was expressed in leaves, roots, stems, and at two floral developmental stages of male, hermaphrodite, and female plants. Expression was markedly higher in flowers, especially in female flowers and their pistils (Supplementary Fig. 13a). The highest expression level was observed in ovules from fruit 5–15 DAP. As ovules developed, expression gradually decreased, with a sharp decline at 35 DAP (Supplementary Fig. 13b).

To further validate spatial expression patterns, we performed in situ hybridization of CpYYL in embryos. Strong hybridization signals were detected in both the early globular embryo and the endotesta at 35 DAP, whereas weaker signals were observed in globular-shaped embryo and endotesta at 50 DAP (Fig. 3a–f), indicated that CpYYL functions in early embryo development.

AtEMB506 protein is localized in the chloroplast, and has a chloroplast targeting signal peptide19. The investigation of subcellular localization of CpYYL displayed CpYYL-GFP was co-localized with the chlorophyll fluorescence signals (Fig. 3i,k), indicating a chloroplast localization. However, when we deleted the putative signal peptide of 41 amino acids directing CpYYL to plastids, CpYYL-del-GFP was irregularly distributed on the cell membrane and not co-localized with the chlorophyll fluorescence signals, confirming the existence of a signal peptide for targeting CpYYL to the chloroplasts (Fig. 3j).

The mutation of CpYYL impacts the expression of genes in sucrose metabolism
To evaluate the impact of CpYYL loss on gene expression, we conducted RNA-seq analysis on ovules at different developmental stages from crosses between “Zhongbai” XX female and XYh hermaphrodites, as well as from self-pollinated XYh hermaphrodites. Because it is not possible to distinguish aborted seeds in self-pollinated hermaphrodite fruit based on phenotype before seed maturation, we included both cross types in the analysis. A total of 50, 524, 801, and 39 DEGs detected at 5, 15, 35, and 65 DAP ovules between ovules of Zhongbai females from the cross and Zhongbai hermaphrodites from self-pollinated plants (Fig. 4a).

We identified 412 and 683 unigenes expressed at 15 and 35 DAP (Fig. 4b). Our focus was on genes specifically expressed at the 15-day stage between female and hermaphrodite ovules. Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis revealed that the downregulated DEGs were mainly enriched in post-embryonic morphogenesis, succinate transport, oxidation-reduction process and hormone stimulus response. In contrast, the upregulated DEGs are primarily associated with precursor metabolites and energy, pyruvate metabolic and glycolytic processes (Fig. 4c). Further analysis using the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) indicated that the downregulated DEGs were mainly enriched in pathways related to carbon fixation via the Calvin cycle, glycolysis, and starch and sucrose metabolism (Fig. 4d).

Sucrose metabolism provide energy for embryonic development20–22. The key enzymes involved in this process, including alkaline/neutral invertases (A/N-Inv-C), which are localized in the mitochondria, and catalyzes the breakdown of sucrose into glucose and fructose, thereby fueling various cellular processes23. Additionally, a suite of other enzymes, including hexokinase 4 (HXK4), cytoplasmic phosphoglucose isomerase (CPGI), PFK3, fructose-1,6-bisphosphate aldolase (FBA6)24, fructokinase (FRK), triosephosphate isomerase (TPI), and fructose-bisphosphate aldolase 6 (FBA6)25, plays significant roles in this metabolic cascade. The genes encoding these enzymes all showed increased transcription in 15-day hermaphrodite ovules (Fig. 4e, f), which in turn accelerates the glycolytic pathway. This metabolic shift is further underscored by the observation of significantly reduced sucrose content in hermaphrodites at the 15-day stage (Fig. 4g, h, Supplementary Fig. 14, and Supplementary Data 4, 5), highlighting the dynamic changes in energy metabolism during this critical developmental phase.

CpYYL interact with CpAKRP during the papaya life cycle
To explore the molecular mechanisms underlying protein interaction involving CpYYL, we screened for potential interacting proteins. Yeast two-hybrid analysis revealed a strong interaction between CpYYL and an ankyrin repeat protein, CpAKRP (Fig. 5a, b). AKRP is crucial in the initial differentiation of the proplastid19. Domain interaction analysis using truncated domains of CpYYL and CpAKRP showed that the interaction was markedly weakened when only the N-terminal regions of both proteins were present, whereas efficient binding required the four ankyrin (ANK) domain repeats along with its upstream region (Supplementary Fig. 15).

Subsequent BiFC-assays confirmed the in vivo interaction between CpYYL and CpAKRP (Fig. 5c). Due to papaya’s two-year transformation cycle, we used transformed Arabidopsis to validate the role of CpAKRP. Overexpression of CpYYL and CpAKRP partially rescued the 25% seed abortion phenotype in the heterozygous emb506 and akrp mutants (Fig. 5d, e).

Population genomic analysis of CpYYL
To investigate the evolutionary history of YYL, we analyzed 63 sequenced plant genomes. The YYL gene predates seed plants, with orthologs identified in algae, liverworts, mosses, and ferns, the earliest evolutionary origin of YYL gene can be traced to Chlamydomonas, highlighting the early origin and evolution of YYL (Supplementary Fig. 16a). Examination of YYL across 63 gymnosperm and angiosperm genomes revealed strong conservation, particularly in the ANK repeat domain associated with protein interactions (Supplementary Data 6 and Supplementary Fig. 16b). The CpYYL-X allele demonstrated was confirmed to be functional based on its intact gene structure and complementation test. In contrast, the cpyyl-h allele is a pseudogene, lacking expression due to the absence of the first exon and part of the first intron. Nucleotide diversity (π) for CpYYL-X was 5.26e-05 in cultivated and 8.33e-05 in wild papaya, whereas for cpyyl-h, it was 2.01e-06 in cultivated and 3.48e-06 in the wild papaya (Supplementary Fig. 17a, b), indicating limited diversity.

Furthermore, the Tajima’s D value for CpYYL-X was -1.34 in cultivated and -1.15 in wild papaya, with FST scores ranging from 0 to 0.1 (Supplementary Fig. 17c–f). These values suggest a potential selection pressure acting on this allele. In contrast, cpyyl-h’s Tajima’s D value was near zero (Supplementary Fig. 17f), indicating that this pseudogene has not been subject to selection pressures due to mutations.

Recombination suppression between HSY and MSY in YYh male papaya
The creation of viable YYh male plants offered an unprecedented opportunity to identify the carpel suppressing sex determination gene in male flowers through forward genetics. “SunUp” females were crossed with 24-6 YYh males and generated a testcross population segregating males to hermaphrodites at 1:1 ratio. Male- and hermaphrodite-specific DNA markers were used to genotyping 537 testcross plants (Supplementary Fig. 18), yielding 294 male and 243 hermaphrodite genotypes, perfectly matching the sex phenotypes with zero recombinant plants (Supplementary Data 7).

We also examined the sex segregation ratio in the offspring of the two test cross 20-1 and 15-4 population (Supplementary Figs. 19 and 20). The 20-1 testcross population consisted of 194 plants, with 110 hermaphrodites and 84 males, while the 15-4 testcross population comprised 483 plants, with 236 hermaphrodites and 247 male plants. Both populations fitted to a 1:1 male to hermaphrodite segregation ratio (Chi-square test, p=0.062 for 20–1 populations and p=0.616 for 15–4 populations).
